speaker_notes.note: The opening of this student intervention is garbled by ASR, but the substantive question is clear: absolute will is being compared to faith and contingent will to belief that still seeks justification.
Jiang appears to repeat 'the contingent will' several times while searching for a simple phrasing; the repetition is ASR-noisy but the intended soul/body distinction is clear.

interactions.summary: Students sharpen the contrast by calling absolute will active, unstoppable, faith-like, God-aligned, and perfect, while contingent will is described as reactive, justification-seeking, misaligned, and imperfect; Jiang keeps pushing for a simpler synthesis.

Jiang finally reduces the distinction to soul versus body: the soul stays linked to God, the body reacts to the material world and can fear, and the human task is to harmonize these many dimensions of will rather than let them split apart.

claims.claim: A student says absolute will is active and unstoppable because it creates its own conditions, while contingent will reacts to the material situation given to it.
Another student proposes that absolute will is more like faith while contingent will is belief that still demands justification.
Students continue to approximate the distinction by saying absolute will is alignment with God or perfection, while contingent will marks misalignment or fault-prone embodiment.

Jiang's simplified account is that absolute will belongs to the soul, which remains connected to God, while contingent will belongs to the body, which must answer the material world and is therefore susceptible to fear.
Jiang uses Piccarda to show that the soul can remain true to God even while the body's fear-driven contingent will defies that truth in action.

When asked whether the two wills can coexist, Jiang answers yes and expands the model: the will exists across infinite dimensions, and a person's task is to bring those dimensions into harmony by aligning contingent will with absolute will.

signature_moments.moment: A student captures absolute will as the force that finds a way and creates its own conditions instead of waiting for permission from circumstances.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it creates its own condition for it is unstoppable
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the class's strongest active-versus-reactive formulation before Jiang compresses the distinction into soul and body.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang's decisive simplification is that absolute will is the soul and contingent will is the body that gets scared by the material universe.
signature_moments.source_phrase: absolute will is a soul ... contingent will is the body
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's core compression and the clearest handle for later read-writing and lens work on agency under coercion.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang abruptly widens the model from two wills to infinite dimensions of will that a person must harmonize.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the will existing in infinite dimensions
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns a local doctrine about coercion into a larger metaphysics of personhood and alignment.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: In Jiang's simplified explanation, the soul's God-facing will that remains oriented toward the good even when bodily fear pulls action elsewhere.
Jiang's expanded model that a person contains many layers of willing and must create harmony among them by aligning contingent responses with the soul's higher orientation.

chronology_notes.note: The packet completes the exploratory definitions from the prior packet and lands on Jiang's own synthesis: from active versus reactive will, to faith versus justification, to the final soul/body model and then the broader idea of harmonizing many dimensions of will.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student's opening words are ASR-garbled, but the usable substance is the faith-versus-belief comparison for absolute and contingent will.
